hook_text: A security gate just taught you the area of ANY triangle — no height needed, no right angle in sight.
clip_script: You know those concertina security gates that fold flat? One diamond cell of that gate is about to hand you a whole grade eleven formula. Two rigid arms, hinged at a corner. Arms at ninety degrees? The cell traps its MAXIMUM space. Start folding the gate — the arms never change length, but the space between them shrinks... and shrinks... until the gate is flat and the space is GONE. That's the area rule in motion: area equals half, times one side, times the other side, times SINE of the angle between them. Sine is the squash factor. At ninety degrees sine is one — no squash, full area, and the formula collapses into the old half base times height. At zero or one-eighty, sine is zero — flat gate, no triangle. So when a question gives you two sides of a plot and the angle where they meet, you don't need any perpendicular height. Six centimetres, eleven centimetres, forty degrees at the hinge? Half times six times eleven times sine forty — about twenty-one comma two square centimetres. Done. One warning: the angle MUST sit between your two sides. Finger on each side — take the angle where your fingers meet. Wrong hinge, wrong squash, wrong area.
visual_style: A neon concertina gate folds and unfolds in a loop; one diamond cell glows with its trapped area shading in and out as the hinge angle sweeps, a sine meter rides from one down to zero, and the formula assembles piece by piece.
pacing: Gate-folding hook, slow-motion squash with the sine meter, rapid formula assembly, sharp fingers-on-sides warning to close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and measure any triangle the gate's way.
